title: Saltmarsh Lowland Ecology and the Crescent Kangaroo

Saltmarsh Lowland Ecology and the Crescent Kangaroo

Abstract

The Verrin Saltmarsh Lowlands support nine to fourteen overwintering troupes of Crescent Kangaroo. We describe the lowland's three sedge zones, the communal mud-wallows used in winter, and the role of troupes in seed dispersal. Wallow sediments retain more moisture and have lower bulk density than adjacent mud, and they support a distinct halotolerant invertebrate assemblage. Feeding trials show that 38% of ingested sedge seeds remain viable after gut passage, with retention times of 19–27 hours, allowing troupes to move propagules one to four kilometres. We argue that overwintering troupes are ecological agents within the lowland disturbance regime, not merely resident herbivores, and that creek straightening and reduced tidal exchange threaten both the sedge mosaic and the wallows.
Keywords: saltmarsh; sedge zonation; mud wallow; seed dispersal; Crescent Kangaroo
1. Introduction

The Verrin Saltmarsh Lowlands occupy a shallow, storm-built embayment on the eastern shore of Marrow Bay, where freshwater seepage meets diurnal tides and produces a mosaic of saline mudflats, low sedge meadows, and stranded wrack ridges. The lowlands are best known as winter range for the Crescent Kangaroo (Macropus lunatus), a medium-sized macropodid whose troupes descend from the dry Cinderwood uplands each November and remain until March. Long-term surveys by Harwell and Osei (2019) recorded between nine and fourteen troupes in the lowlands, with group sizes of six to twenty-two animals. Their arrival coincides with the senescence of the dominant sedges and the exposure of seed heads along the tidal creeks, a seasonal overlap that has shaped both the vegetation and the animals' winter ecology.
2. Sedge zonation

The salt-tolerant sedge communities form three broad zones. Lower marsh, flooded on most high tides, is dominated by Carex salinofirma and Schoenoplectus halophilus, both of which tolerate soil salinities above 28 ppt and accumulate dense root mats that bind the mud. Mid-marsh supports Juncus caesariensis and a short-statured form of Carex salinofirma, while the upper marsh grades into brackish meadow with Eleocharis pseudohalophila. These zones are not fixed. Storms and creek migration reset patches of vegetation, and the resulting mosaic is important to overwintering kangaroos because it offers adjacent feeding, resting, and wallowing habitat. Mbeki (2007) argued that the lowland sedges are edaphic specialists rather than tide specialists, and subsequent transplant experiments by Lin and colleagues (2016) supported that view.

3. Mud-wallowing

Mud-wallowing is a conspicuous winter behavior. Troupes establish communal wallows in soft intertidal pans, usually where a creek meander has deposited fine silt and clay. Animals roll and knead the sediment, then rest in shallow basins that retain water for several hours after the tide falls. The behavior has been interpreted chiefly as ectoparasite control, since mud coating reduces tick loads and perhaps masks scent during the winter mobbing season. It also has ecological consequences. Repeated trampling homogenizes the surface sediment, creates small depressions that trap seeds and organic matter, and aerates the upper mud during low tide. Osei (2012) found that wallow sediments had higher moisture and lower bulk density than adjacent unvisited mud, and that the wallows supported a distinct assemblage of halotolerant invertebrates.
4. Seed dispersal

Seed dispersal is the troupe's most important indirect effect on the lowland flora. Crescent Kangaroos graze sedge culms and seed heads through the winter, and their broad diet includes Carex salinofirma, Juncus caesariensis, and at least four associated marsh forbs. Feeding trials by Feldman and Iyer (2014) showed that 38 percent of ingested sedge seeds remained viable after gut passage, with mean retention times of 19 to 27 hours. Because troupes move between creek-side meadows, salt pans, and upland edges, they can carry propagules one to four kilometres from source patches. Most seeds are deposited in latrine sites and muddy resting areas, where germination is often higher than on undisturbed marsh surface. In this way the kangaroos may reinforce the patchy advance of sedges along retreating creek banks, although the effect varies with winter rainfall and tide height.
5. Discussion

Together, these interactions place the Crescent Kangaroo within the lowland's disturbance regime rather than outside it. The sedge communities provide winter forage and cover, the wallows concentrate nutrients and moisture, and seed dispersal links otherwise isolated vegetation patches. Conservation planning for the Verrin Saltmarsh Lowlands should therefore treat overwintering troupes as ecological agents, not merely as resident herbivores. Hydrological modification, especially creek straightening and reduced tidal exchange, threatens both the sedge zonation and the muddy wallows on which the troupes depend. Continued monitoring by the Marrow Bay Ecological Survey, initiated in 1988, will be essential if the winter ecology of this unusual lowland system is to be understood before further change occurs.
